speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: REPORT RESPECTING RECORDED INTERVIEW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of personal privilege. In the debate on the amendment to the Old Age Security Act two evenings ago there was an unfortunate reluctance by some members opposite, and in particular the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), to accept my word with respect to an alleged tape recorded interview which had been held and published in last Friday's issue of the Toronto Globe and Mail. I beg to call to the attention of the house, and particularly the hon. member, a report which appears on the front page of today's issue of the Globe and Mail. I wish, sir, to read it into the record. It is as follows:
Health minister Judy LaMarsh has denied in the commons that she suggested there were any grounds for accusing the Lesage government in Quebec as "Nazi-to-be". Thanking the member who gave her the opportunity to make the denial, Miss LaMarsh said she had never made such a statement at any time to anyone.
The issue arose as the result of an interview on the subject of pensions which Miss LaMarsh had given to a staff writer of the Globe and Mail. The interview was published in Friday editions of this newspaper.
A report in Wednesday's editions of the Globe and Mail on the commons exchange stated erroneously that a tape recorder had been used during the interview. While the newspaper had considered the possibility of recording the interview and while this possibility had been mentioned to Miss LaMarsh, no tape recorder was used. The Globe and Mail regrets this error in its account of the debate and any embarrassment it may have caused Miss LaMarsh.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE RIVER-THREATENED STRIKE OF LONGSHOREMEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour and ask him what is the present position with respect to the threatened strike by the longshoremen. What action is being taken, and what are the hopes of this dispute being settled?

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE RIVER-THREATENED STRIKE OF LONGSHOREMEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the special mediator appointed to deal with this matter has met with the shipping federation, and he also met separately with the longshoremen. I understand he has a meeting this afternoon with both groups, and at that meeting he will attempt to mediate the differences between the two parties concerned. I think we must give Judge Lippe an opportunity to exhaust all possibilities in the process of mediation before undertaking any further action at this time.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE RIVER-THREATENED STRIKE OF LONGSHOREMEN
speechtext: In the event that there is not a settlement, has the government a plan in mind to prevent this very serious situation developing?

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE RIVER-THREATENED STRIKE OF LONGSHOREMEN
speechtext: I think the situation is serious in light of a possible strike. It ought to be realized that any strike contemplated is fully lawful in the situation, because it would occur after a seven day interval following the report of the conciliation board. However, the government is keeping a very careful watch on the situation and will decide what steps should be taken in the event of any breakdown in the mediation process. But I think it would be premature to assume at this stage that they will be unsuccessful in reaching a settlement.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Labour whether he can advise the house what the delay is in dealing with the great lakes situation, and when is the government expecting to take action in order to resolve this serious situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has placed on the order paper at the earliest possible moment a resolution providing for the introduction of legislation for the establishment of a public trusteeship. Under our parliamentary process today would be the first day that it would be possible to deal with that matter. However, a very intensive consideration of this problem is being undertaken today in Ottawa. The under secretary of labour for the United States, Mr. Reynolds, has been in Ottawa since ten o'clock this

Inquiries oj the Ministry morning; discussions are going on and contact is being maintained from this central discussion with other groups in the search for an inter-union settlement. In those circumstances it would be my view that it would be premature to proceed until all the possibilities for an inter-union settlement have been exhausted.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: A supplementary question. In view of what the minister has said, are we to believe that it is now left to the United States government to resolve this dispute?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government realizes the importance and seriousness of this matter and has been acting in a very constructive and determined way since the receipt of the Norris commission report. On the other hand, as I have said already, the government intends to proceed with this legislation unless a solid and effective alternative is presented. The Canadian labour movement, I am sure, is quite capable of deciding what should be done in consultation with the Canadian government, and the government is quite capable, following such consultation, of deciding what is an effective and solid alternative. I think it would be irresponsible in the situation not to allow for the possibility of an inter-union arrangement in which the Canadian Labour Congress would be a full participant.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Labour a further supplementary question. What is the role of the undersecretary of labour for the United States in this dispute, since he is here in Canada?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: I think it has been obvious for some months now that the good offices of the undersecretary of labour of the United States have been available to assist in the settlement of the situation which, as the hon. member knows, has very serious international implications. The secretary of labour and his under secretary have lent their good offices in the search for this solid, effective alternative in the form of an inter-union arrangement.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Newspaper reports suggest that the Minister of Labour is bringing pressure on Canadian trade union leaders to accept a private trusteeship in which the final appeal will be to the A.F. of L.-C.I.O. labour movement of the United States. I want to ask the minister first whether he will deny that; and second, whether he will assure the house that if government trusteeship legislation is abandoned we can be sure that any private trusteeship will be effective, and that it will be


vested in Canada and under the control of the Canadian labour movement?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext:
I think it is altogether false to suggest that the Minister of Labour of Canada has put any pressure on the officers of the Canadian Labour Congress to accept any such settlement, and I believe the officers of the Canadian Labour Congress would be the first to admit that I have consulted them in a spirit of responsibility at every stage of these negotiations. The Canadian Labour Congress and the various labour bodies concerned in Canada will obviously be permitted to express their views and to make their own decisions, because any alternative to government action will provide for an arrangement between the two labour sectors, one in the United States and one in Canada; and surely it is not the purpose of the Canadian government to put pressure on the C.L.C. to reach a decision which in its judgment would be contrary to its best interests.
I can assure the hon. member that our purpose in this situation is to establish an effective alternative if possible. If that should not be possible the government will proceed with its public trusteeship legislation. I assure hon. members there will be no disposition on the part of the Canadian government to enter into an arrangement, or withdraw, in this situation if the alternative in our judgment would not be effective, or fail to protect Canadian interests.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext:
A further supplementary
question. May I ask the minister if he himself has seen the United States under secretary of labour, or if the latter is here for the purpose of exerting such pressure as he may choose on the Canadian trade union leaders?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I saw Mr. Reynolds this morning and had a discussion with him in which we reviewed the situation. To my knowledge the under secretary has had no direct contact with the officers of the Canadian Labour Congress, and in the circumstances any contact would be undertaken, at least initially, through officials of my department or myself. I wish to assure the hon. member that the under secretary of labour has come to Canada as the result of a request which I made to the secretary of labour of the United States that an honest search should be continued toward a solution of this difficult question. We are honestly searching to find out what alternatives may still remain and whether the differences may be reconciled. That is the purpose of the under secretary's visit. There is certainly no intention that he come here to exert pressure on the Canadian government or the Canadian Labour Congress.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad the hon. member brought this question up again, because we have been discussing the removal of the quota on turkeys since last spring.
On August 21 it was decided that this should be done, and an order in council was passed on August 26 to this effect. Our reason for doing this was that turkeys imported into Canada are protected by a tariff of 5 cents per pound, and also the fact that the discounted dollar provides for another 2J cents per pound protection which, plus the freight, amounts to something like 9 cents per pound before United States turkeys compete with Canadian turkeys.

Mr. Chairman, I understood that that was usually given when the bill was before the committee, but I will be glad to do it now. This resolution provides two twelfths of the items in the main and supplementary estimates tabled prior to the adjournment and includes eight twelfths of the supplementary estimates tabled yesterday, bringing the total supply which would be released to date up to eight twelfths of the total estimates if the bill is passed. When the bill is presented it will also include additional borrowing authority up to $500 million. I should like to assure the committee that the proportions requested in the bill, as hon. members will see when it is before the committee, are intended to provide for all necessary requirements of the public service up to November 30, 1963. In no instance is the total amount of an item being released by the bill. The form of this bill is the usual one for interim supply bills, and the passing of this bill will not prejudice the rights and privileges of hon. members to question or criticize any item in the estimates when it comes up for consideration. The usual undertaking is hereby given that such rights and privileges will be respected and will not be curtailed or restricted in any way as a result of the passing of this measure.

I should like to thank the minister for his most helpful and useful statement. Before this committee votes interim supply it is my duty and my purpose to bring to the notice of hon. members certain recent developments in this country, developments which, in the opinion of the majority of our members on this side of the house, if continued will have serious effects on Canada and on all Canadians.
These developments relate to the total collapse of the majority of the government's major legislative proposals as contained in the speech from the throne. They relate, in fact, to the total collapse of the Pearson plan for moving our economy ahead and for upholding the myth of improving Canada's prestige abroad.
Why has such a collapse taken place? Many Canadians of all political stripes are asking

Interim Supply
this question today. It has happened because the government, by its dictatorial arrogance and by its lack of consultation with the people and with local authorities during its short time in office, has lost touch with reality and with the people of Canada.
In my brief remarks this afternoon I should like to touch with equal brevity on some background historical material. During the war years and the post-war years, Canadians willingly gave up many of their normal freedoms in order to bring the world conflict to a successful conclusion. In the fifties the Liberal establishment was denied by the people of Canada, speaking through their duly elected members in this House of Commons, the possession of complete emergency powers forever. That was in 1956 and 1957. One would have thought the Grits would have learned their lesson. Yet the dictatorial arrogance of 1956 and 1957 was only a minor tune as compared with the symphony of confusion we have today. I say that the Pearson-Gordon-LaMarsh attitude must go. Canadians of all parties-and this includes Liberals, Conservatives and members of other political parties from the Atlantic to the Pacific- demand that it should go for the good of Canada.
Many people in Canada today say they see little difference in the approach of the political parties to major public issues. Perhaps that is something for which all members in this house are to blame to a greater or lesser degree. Nevertheless, for those of us who have examined Liberal doctrine and the position taken by the Grits, there is no difficulty in discovering the reason for contemporary confusion. Only the other day backbenchers of the party opposite castigated the cabinet in general and individual ministers in particular. I am sure this is the first time in the history of modern democracy that a ministry has been castigated by its backbenchers for losing touch not only with the people of Canada but with its own supporters in parliament.
There is another matter which I think should be brought up again and again both on the floor of the chamber and outside; something which will make clear beyond doubt the difference between the political parties in this country today, a difference which will soon become readily apparent to all Canadians. The hon. lady who a number of weeks ago proposed or seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne enunciated a Liberal collectivist theory which was not denied by anyone in the Liberal high command. This theory means, in essence, that the individual today does not count in the eyes of the government; he does not know what is good for him. According to this

theory the Liberal establishment will tell him what is good for him, and government decisions will be enforced in every locality whether wanted or not.
What happened yesterday? We asked the Minister of Labour whether, before he decreed that certain municipalities were to be declared depressed areas, the local authorities had been consulted in advance. The minister did not answer because he knew the local authorities had not been consulted. These municipalities are to be declared depressed areas whether they want it or not, merely because someone here in Ottawa has a chart which says they must be called depressed areas. Lack of consultation is one of the major reasons why the whole government's domestic program is on the rocks. Arrogance, lack of humility and lack of consultation have produced this situation. I notice the superior attitude of the President of the Privy Council. He looks across at me as if I were a young school boy who knows nothing about the intricacies of the planners. I say to him that planning or no planning, in a confederation such as Canada you should consult the local authorities before superimposing decisions on them from the top.
Before I catalogue in some detail the results of this attitude there is another thing I should like to say. It relates to our great civil service. But before I bring this subject to the attention of our members, and to make sure that responsibility will surround the debate in this regard, I wish to say that in my opinion Canada happens to be blessed with one of the finest civil services in the free world. Nothing that I have to say relates to any desire on my part to amend the Civil Service Act or the departmental regulations concerning political activity in the civil service. I want to make that perfectly clear before I proceed with the remarks I wish to make.
Having said that, I wish to emphasize and re-emphasize that we are witnessing a phenomenon which I think is unprecedented in parliamentary history in the modern western world, namely the composition of the ministry which is before us today. The Liberal ministry of today is made up to the extent of more than one third, of former senior civil servants.
I do not intend to suggest that this in itself is a bad thing, but I am going to say this; that in Canada today under the parliamentary system, Montesquieu's separation of powers theory does not necessarily, in toto or in part, apply to parliamentary democracy. We in the Canadian parliament only have true freedom when there is a real separation between the administrative and legislative wings of government and I maintain that with the present ministry, one third of which is composed of

former senior bureaucrats, we do not have that desirable state of freedom today. Having already said, and I reiterate, that we have in Canada one of the finest civil services in the western world, I say that this point must be placed again and again before the people of Canada.
I have often talked to the Secretary of State privately and I know he feels that I belabour this point to an absurd degree, but I think this situation must be looked at seriously today regardless of any consideration of amendments to the Civil Service Act or departmental regulations.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Could the hon. gentleman repeat that sentence? I apologize to him. As he knows, I have one deaf ear and I was giving the other to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

Since I am not reading from a text it is hard for me to go back. I will never forget the spectacle of the Prime Minister meeting all the deputy ministers after the election. I thought this was a very poor move. It was as if he was saying "Hello, boys, here we are again; we are the only establishment you can ever work with for the good of Canada". What palpably absurd nonsense. No matter how much yelling I hear from the opposite benches I am going to bring this point before the house and the people of Canada time and time again.
I have brought the point before the House of Commons that much of the Liberal economic program has foundered on the rocks because of a lack of consultation with local authorities and the people. It has always been a Conservative principle to put emphasis on the wishes of the people and the dignity of the individual. We realize that in our federal union, to dictate from Ottawa without consulting the local authorities crushes individual initiative and spells disaster.
I am not thinging about this only for today, Mr. Chairman. Burke, one of the great founders of Conservative principles, placed great emphasis on the importance of local self-agency. This is a principle or doctrine that Liberalism has never been able to claim, so let us not be surprised at what is happening today. The people of Canada should recognize this difference in principle. Burke's idea of local self-agency is a principle which is very important to Canadian Conservatism in 1963.
In the speech from the throne we heard about the notion of co-operative federalism. As far as most members on this side of the house are concerned, co-operative federalism denotes a high degree of consultation. What have we seen in the few short months since? I put this straight question to the
Interim Supply
Minister of National Health and Welfare. When the hon. lady introduced the universal contributory pension scheme on the floor of the House of Commons on July 18 last was she aware-yes or no-of Mr. Lesage's intentions, either from her colleagues in the cabinet or through reading the province of Quebec press? If she was aware, why did she go blindly ahead? This question has not been answered. Here again we have a lack of co-operation and a lack of consultation with the provinces.
The Minister of Labour admitted that he did not consult the Minister of Finance before he brought in the $500 bonus for home builders. I asked the Minister of Labour repeatedly yesterday, do you intend to consult the municipalities before declaring that they are depressed areas? I did not get an answer. Why? Because Liberal doctrine dictates that there is no consultation. Whether or not the municipality wants to be designated a depressed area, it is going to be called one. Under our administration we did not call them distressed areas; they were labour surplus areas. The legislation was made public and situations were dealt with on the basis of local initiative.
Surely the Minister of Finance must realize that his budget and the major economic measures he intended to introduce on the floor of the House of Commons-hon. members may laugh, but these are the facts and the people of Canada know them-to move the economy ahead floundered. Why? Because of a lack of consultation. With regard to the municipal loans legislation there was no consultation with local authorities or the provinces. In respect of the budget there was no consultation with senior civil servants. It is no wonder that because of a lack of consultation an integral part of the whole economic program of the government has floundered, much to the regret of all Canadians who put country before party.
I hope that never again will a tax be levied and then revised as was done in the case of the tax on building materials. I am not going into details in this regard.
However, the retail lumbermen's association met in Vancouver last week, and its members were most alarmed at the slow-down in construction which is directly attributable to this tax. In the city of Calgary alone construction has declined by $30 million in the period from June 14 until now compared with a similar period last year.
Much to our incredible surprise we also see no consultation among the cabinet ministers themselves. The Prime Minister says that the health plan should be submitted to a parliamentary committee. The Minister of National

Interim Supply
Health and Welfare says that she hopes it will not be and it should not be. We hear free trade doctrines coming out of the mouth of the Minister of Trade and Commerce while on the other hand the new Minister of Industry preaches protectionism.
Every Canadian wants to see the world fair under way and preparations completed on time, but look at the confusion and lack of consultation that have existed up until now. Just the other day a suggestion emanated from the government that they may name a Liberal backbencher as a liaison officer between the authorities in Montreal and Ottawa. Will this add more confusion to the confusion already existing? We do not know, but we do know that many of the difficulties with regard to the world fair up to now have been caused by a lack of consultation. That is a phrase I am reiterating time and time again in my brief speech this afternoon.
A few weeks ago I asked the Minister of Agriculture whether before designating areas for ARDA projects the local authorities were consulted. The minister could not even give me an answer. In every country in the western world with legislation like ARDA the programs are based on the idea of local initiative, but even after repeated questioning the Minister of Agriculture could not guarantee to the house that ARDA projects would be designated only after consultation with the local authorities.
I am not taking sides at the present time in the classical debate of centralization versus provincial rights, but whether you feel that Canada is in danger of being balkanized too much or whether you feel that Canada should not have too much central government, no matter what side you take in this debate, I think all hon. members recognize the desirability of setting up within a very short time some sort of agency or secretariat for federal-provincial relations.
I say, and many members have said inside and outside this house, that such an agency or secretariat will not necessarily solve all the problems, but it will go a long way toward helping to channel communication with different levels of government. I say to the ministry opposite in the name of the people governed, first of all let us consult local authorities. Let us all realize that the original Pearson myth for improving our image abroad is long dead, as the Pearson plan for moving our economy ahead is dead. Mr. Chairman, I am availing myself of the first opportunity which has presented itself since parliament reassembled to register a protest against the action of the government in entering into an agreement with the United States for the acceptance of nuclear weapons for Canadian forces without submitting this agreement to parliament. Indeed, the government has gone much further and has refused to allow parliament to see the agreement upon which this commitment is based. The only document we have which tells us anything about this agreement is the official communique issued by the Prime Minister's office, and therefore I think I should place it on the record since it is, as I say, the only document we have giving us any information at all. It is dated August 16, 1963 and says:
The Right Hon. L. B. Pearson, Prime Minister, announced today that as a result of negotiations begun three years ago and resumed by the present Canadian government after taking office the Canadian and United States governments have reached agreement on the conditions under which nuclear warheads will be made available for Canadian forces engaged in North American defence and assigned to NATO. The weapons systems affected are the "Bomarc B", the Voodoo interceptor, the Honest John artillery rocket and the CF-104 Starfighter strike-reconnaissance aircraft.
In accordance with the requirements of national security and with NATO practice, details will not be published. The arrangements relating to custody and control satisfactorily protect Canada's national interest and conform with the position Canada has taken internationally on the non-dissemination of nuclear weapons.
When the stockpiles are established the warheads will remain in United States custody, and for this purpose small units of United States custodial personnel will be stationed at the Canadian storage sites at bases which will, of course, remain under Canadian command and control. With custody remaining with the United States the arrangement does not add to the numbers of governments having nuclear weapons at their independent disposal. It is also to be noted that provision is made for the application at all times of the most stringent safety measures. Finally, these nuclear warheads cannot be used operationally without the authorization of the Canadian government. Joint control is thus assured.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I want to make two points with reference to this statement. The first is that the Canadian government has no right under our parliamentary democratic system to make commitments on behalf of the Canadian people without the approval of parliament. This agreement between Canada and the United States does three things. First, it commits Canada to accept nuclear warheads from the United States. Second, it requires Canada to station United States military

It is clear, as the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau) so properly said that we, in Quebec, want the matter to be settled once and for all so we may stop talking about it.
The sponsor of the bill may be assured of my support. Unfortunately, he lingered, as usual, over political and partisan considerations and, therefore, incurred a rather sharp reply from his opponent. I deplore such things, but I may assure him of my support as member for Lake St. John.
I approve the bill because, to my mind, it is excellent and will have splendid results. It will enable us to keep a small part of that revenue which flows regularly out of this country every year. Some people may be somewhat embarrassed about the situation, but I think that lottery tickets are sold in all Canadian provinces. We see, from press reports, that individuals, residing from Vancouver to Halifax make considerable profits at this game. This means that lotteries are accepted by people, in a general way, everywhere in Canada.
I think that an amendment to the Criminal Code would enable those provinces who wish to do so to pass a similar legislation and insert it in their own statutes. This would be a true observance of provincial autonomy which would enable the provinces to make their own decisions in the matter.
That is all I have to say and as I have already said, I support the bill.

speechtext:
should like to add a few words to the discussion of this proposed legislation. I think

the measure before us is non-political in the sense that members in all parties have their own views for or against the principle of extending the licensing of lotteries. I am in favour of the proposal which is before us. I am in favour of extending government control over sweepstakes and lotteries. It seems to me that when thousands of Canadians participate every year in the purchase of lottery and sweepstake tickets, with the result that millions of dollars leave our country, a situation is created which might well be remedied by legislation such as is before us. Indeed, money would be encouraged to flow into the provinces from sources outside this country as people abroad bought Canadian sweepstake or lottery tickets.
As things stand we already have in Canada something like 28 operations which are in conflict with the present law. The results of public opinion polls across the country continue to show that in a large measure the public would support the steps contemplated in the bill now before us. It represents, of course, a step toward government operation and legalization of sweepstakes. I am opposed, as are other members of my party, to hospital or educational boards setting themselves up to derive direct benefit from the sale of lottery tickets. Like my colleagues, I think this field should be strictly one for taxation. However, I approve the idea of extending to the provinces the right to license lotteries which would bring in money for general revenue purposes. It is clear we have already accepted in principle in the various provinces the idea of sweepstakes or lotteries, whether it is churches which promote bingo games or governments which derive provincial revenue from the operation of such things as parimutuel racing. Extension to the provinces of the right to run sweepstakes and lotteries would simply provide for a do-it-yourself tax which would allow the people to have a little fun while contributing something to provincial revenues.
I have much satisfaction in supporting the proposal before us. Having said that, I shall resume my seat in the hope that the house may be encouraged to come to a vote.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising at this time I should like to advise the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) at the outset that I am 100 per cent in favour of his motion. I sincerely hope the government headed by our present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) will bring in laws and regulations to enact this bill, that is, to amend the Criminal Code so that the attorneys general of the provinces may authorize sweepstakes on behalf of universities and hospitals.

I must say, however, it seems somewhat ridiculous that we should be debating a principle which is largely accepted throughout the country, even though it may not have been legalized. No fewer than three members of the federal cabinet have already admitted by their actions that drawings or lotteries are acceptable to them. There was an occasion not so long ago when a member of the cabinet rose in his place and reporting on two identical bids which had been received in respect of a large amount of concrete necessary for the South Saskatchewan dam, advised this house that since he did not know how to settle the question he intended to put the two bids in a hat and make a drawing. Drawings and lotteries are the same thing.
Another cabinet minister, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) himself, the hon. gentleman who is responsible for enforcing the Criminal Code, has also expressed an attitude, if only indirectly. I was interested to read in the Ottawa Journal, a paper which is widely read by hon. members of the house, an article on June 26 listing the names of three holders of Irish sweepstakes tickets. Included among the list of ticket holders printed on page 41 of that newspaper we find, in the second paragraph:
One of the ticket holders in Cyril Rich, 34, 41 Ashburn Drive, an employee of the Justice Department. He holds a ticket on Vic Mo Chroi.
I personally drew the matter to the attention of the Minister of Justice and I wondered whether the hon. gentleman would be congratulating Mr. Rich for having secured a lucky ticket or whether he would be condemning the man for breaking the law of the land. I received a smile in reply. A day or two later a picture of Mr. Rich appeared in the Ottawa Citizen, again giving his name and address. He had won something like $30,000. My congratulations to him. I would simply point out that the Minister of Justice took no action and we can therefore take it that what is being done by the people of Canada in this regard is being condoned by the Department of Justice. Frankly, I should like to see their actions legalized.
Then we come to the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill). He, too, approves lotteries, drawings, or games of chance. We have a member sitting in this house today who was elected on the flip of a coin, as was admitted in a widely publicized statement by the returning officer. If this hon. gentleman can hold his seat on the flip of a coin after all that publicity, and if the Secretary of State takes no action, I maintain that yet another member of the cabinet is approving games of chance and is in favour of altering the aspect
Sweepstakes
of the law with regard to lotteries which Mr. Pigeon would like to have legalized throughout Canada.

speechtext:
I have in my hand three tickets on the Cambridgeshire, the date of which is to be announced in the public press any day. I know of no reason why I should conceal the fact that as a member of parliament I buy these tickets. I would point out that in two of the provinces of Canada the attorneys general are now conducting lotteries. I am not the greatest moose hunter in the world but I am an ardent one and I have had many a happy fall hunting season in the area which is represented by my good friend, the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel). I have often hunted there and I expect to hunt again this year.
When I was speaking the other day to a member from New Brunswick about my moose hunting hopes for this fall he said to me, "You are lucky; you must have won the lottery". I said to him, "Lottery? What has that got to do with moose hunting?" He said, "Down in New Brunswick people who want to go moose hunting are so numerous that the government of the province regulates them. These people make application for the right to hunt, send in their fee, a drawing is made by the New Brunswick government and the first couple of hundred names drawn are given moose hunting licenses." People win the opportunity of going moose hunting in the province of New Brunswick. This has been going on for some years and it is known as a draw in the province of New Brunswick.
I hold in my hand page 4 of yesterday's Montreal Gazette. The Canadian Press reports from Quebec city that 37 moose have already been killed in Laurentide park, but the interesting thing about this story is the last two sentences.
The Quebec government has allowed a special short season in the park since last year. Only 300 hunters are allowed into the park, and they are chosen by lot before the season opens.
If the law forbids attorneys general to conduct lotteries, I wonder under what pretence the attorneys general of New Brunswick and Quebec are O.K.'ing the drawing by lot of moose hunting licences in those two areas.
In the province of Ontario the little town of Penetanguishene on Georgian bay has organized, as a wonderful pastime and business developer, one of the largest and greatest winter carnivals held annually in Canada. It

Sweepstakes
is now in its seventh or eighth year, and each year thousands of people come. The feature of this winter carnival is fishing through the ice. For $1 the people who come there are given the necessary bait, a small fishing line and a small rod and they fish through the ice for a period of two hours. The person catching the largest fish wins a boat and outboard motor valued at over $1,000.
Some people who did not like the idea of a boat and motor being given away for the largest fish protested the matter to the attorney general of the province of Ontario. I should like to tell you what the Hon. Kelso Roberts, attorney general of Ontario at that time, had to say. He said that the Pene-tanguishene winter carnival, where a boat and motor are given away for the largest fish produced in the fishing derby, is "the largest legal lottery in Canada" and he was unable to take any action as attorney general of Ontario because in his opinion it was legal. He termed it "the largest legal lottery in Canada".
I would also refer to Ralph Day, a former mayor of the city of Toronto where I reside, and who is still prominent in public life. At one time he was the chief magistrate of the city, and I emphasize the fact that he was the chief magistrate. However, after his term in office was over and he retired into the shade, where ex-mayors reside he bought some Irish sweepstake tickets, as I do and as I believe the majority of Canadians do, and he won a $100,000 prize. My hat is off to the ex-chief magistrate of the city of Toronto. I welcome his good fortune. I trust he has enjoyed his winnings. But I ask hon. members: What action has the federal government taken against the former chief magistrate of the city of Toronto? It is no trouble to find him. Everybody knows where he is. He is a member of the Toronto Transit Commission at present and the government could locate him without any difficulty whatsoever.
I have shown that the purchase of lottery tickets or taking part in drawings is recognized by Canadians from coast to coast and I have mentioned men prominent in public life who should know this is against the Criminal Code. I might point out that at the first Penetanguishene winter carnival the boat and motor were presented to the successful winner, a resident of the city of Barrie, by the then deputy speaker of the House of Commons, the late William Robinson. Following his death his constituency has been represented by the present member and I should like to point out that the hon. member for Simcoe East (Dr. Rynard) has always been a regular attendant at the Penetanguishene winter carnival along with me. We enjoy the

day we spend together at Canada's largest legal lottery.
After 40 years in the newspaper business I do not care to mention the names of newspapers, but another interesting aspect with regard to lotteries is that some of these papers write thundering editorials condemning lotteries as a terrible drain on the public purse and a detriment to the morals of the nation. The papers that write the most thundering editorials, of course, are the ones that run the numbers of the tickets drawn in the Irish sweepstakes in order that they may increase the sales of their papers.
In fact, I know of one paper that every year sells thousands of extra copies to one of the biggest sweepstakes tickets operators in Canada. He has an interesting use for these papers. He mails them to the United States because they contain a list of the numbered tickets drawn. It is illegal in the United States for any newspaper to publish the numbers of the successful tickets in draws, so this man takes these Canadian newspapers and mails them to his sales agents in the United States, of whom there are thousands. He says, for example, "See, in the state of Ohio you are selling tickets numbered A1267532 and so on, and you will notice that tickets very close to that number are in the list in this Canadian paper I have sent you. Show it to the people in Ohio so they will know they are getting the real McCoy and are buying the real Irish sweepstakes tickets." The amazing thing is that this paper, which sells thousands of extra copies, at the same time condemns lotteries as being immoral.
Most hon. members know that in 1956 Great Britain introduced national premium bonds. I have here the parliamentary debates for April and May, 1956 at which time Prime Minister Macmillan introduced the national premium bonds and it can be seen here that Lady Tweedsmuir endorsed them and persuaded Mr. Macmillan to expand the sale of these bonds into the commonwealth countries. She said that their sale in commonwealth countries would tighten the bonds of empire. Maybe it does but, as a former speaker said, it takes money out of Canada which remains in Great Britain for some years.
These premium bonds bear no interest. Those who buy them do so on the basis of chance. It is all right for the moralists to tell you and me that is is wrong to rely on chance. True. In the ninth chapter of Ecclesiastes we read in the tenth verse:
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might.
That is a good injunction and I hope all will take it to heart. But in the very next

verse the writer of Ecclesiastes, the wisest man that ever lived, says:
I saw... that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all.
All my life I have been forced to listen to longwinded statements by puritans decrying the evil influences that would emanate from the legalizing of lotteries in Canada, which influences would in time undermine the entire moral fabric of our Canadian nation and ultimately lead to the disappearance of this great country as we know it. Always these puritanical folk have stressed that if only the people of this country would follow the Biblical injunction to tithe their earnings every week then, ipso facto, there would be more than enough money for all good works, including hospitals and universities as mentioned in this bill. But, they urge, if people are allowed to purchase lottery tickets, then they would not accept the obligation to tithe their earnings and the country would suffer from the lack of good works.
All my life I have been hearing this sort of argument, and all my life the taxes imposed on the people by themselves-because in a democracy all taxes are in the final analysis imposed on the people by the people-have been climbing and climbing and climbing. Now they have reached such a point that today finance ministers and provincial treasurers reiterate that the rate of taxation has finally reached the breaking point find they do not know where to turn for more revenue. But I would point out to you, Mr. Speaker, and to all within the sound of my voice, that as the years have rolled along more and more of the good works that are demanded of us are being performed by the people under the heading of taxation, rather than church givings. If you will stop to analyse the division of the moneys raised in taxes today you will be amazed and pleasurably surprised at the vast amounts that are devoted to good works.
Gone are the days when hospitals are erected only under the protection of religious organizations. Gone are the days when a hungry man could only hope for succor by calling at the parsonages or rectories of the nation. Gone are the days when instruction could only be secured from the educated clergy who introduced schools and universities in this country. Today the cost of hospitals comes primarily out of the taxes of the country. Our annual levies are spent in erecting schoolhouses and universities across the land and relief or welfare is available to those in need from government operated agencies.
Sweepstakes
If you will consider the vast amounts of money spent today by municipal, provincial and federal governments in the dispensation of welfare, in the administration of justice, in the relief of widows, orphaned children, prisoner rehabilitation, workmen's compensation, unemployment insurance, safety on the waterways of Canada, safety on the highways, you will see that God-fearing Canadians from coast to coast are to be counted "among the blessed of our Father, for their works do follow them."
Paul tells us in his great epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 7, verse 5, "They . . . who receive the office of the priesthood have a commandment to take tithes of the people", and in the 27th chapter of Leviticus we read, "And all the tithe of the land whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the tree is the Lord's; it is holy unto the Lord".
The practice of tithing is a blessed one but we are also urged "to heal the sick, cleanse the lepers." We are advised in St. Matthew's gospel that on judgment day the Lord shall say to many, "Come ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world for ... I was sick and ye visited me . . . Then shall the righteous answer him saying: Lord, .	.	.
when saw we thee sick . . . and came unto thee? And the King shall answer and say unto them, verily I say unto you, inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." In all reverence I say that the Lord will not ask you whether you tithed through a church or paid for your good works through taxes which were devoted to good works, but will bless you for having healed the sick, cleansed the lepers and visited the fatherless in their affliction, even if it was under the guise of government operated welfare agencies.
I say, Mr. Speaker, with unlimited admiration for the people of Canada, that if they are given due recognition for the manner in which they spend their income through taxes for good works they are tithing every day and every year. Statisticians provoke me when I read from time to time that one of them has uncovered the fact from income tax reports that the charitable givings of the people of Canada are 2 per cent or 3 per cent or some such distressingly low figure. But do those long-faced mathematicians stop for a moment to calculate how much of the income of those income tax paying Canadians has already been spent in charitable endeavours through the medium of their municipal, provincial or federal governments? Seldom if ever, I have to answer.
Surely, if the taxpayers of Canada are meeting their obligation of tithing through

Sweepstakes
their own taxes, the tax exemptions which they grant to churches and local charities and the share they pay of corporation taxes, plus their givings, they are entitled to "a little flutter" for themselves, if they so choose. I support the bill wholeheartedly.

I do want to bring before the house a little of the history of lottery legislation which I think might be pertinent and interesting to the members of the house before they go so far as to vote on the bill.
In my research, Mr. Speaker, I determined that the first time that lotteries were ever invoked by any government was by the government of France in the early eighteenth century. They were suggested to the government of France, in fact propounded and operated for the government of France, by a gentleman by the name of Casanova who is better known for activities of another type. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether there is any affinity between the sponsor of this bill in this house and his historical antecedent Casanova, who introduced the bill before the government of France. I point out that in a book in which Casanova tells how he introduced this bill to the government of France he says he was enjoined to raise $30 million for a military school. The government wished to get this sum without a charge on the state or emptying the treasury. Casanova answered that it was God alone who had the creative power. Casanova, out of his genius, evolved a lottery such as the hon. gentleman is doing here and obviously he, along with Casanova, has the divine, creative power.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, in challenging the refusal of the government to table the storage warheads agreement of August 16, has cited the United Kingdom Polaris agreement which contains 11 pages of detailed information. I say to him that this is quite a different matter and one that does not involve the disclosure of classified information. It deals with the acquisition of weapons delivery systems and is comparable to our unclassified agreements with the United States to acquire the Bomarc and the Voodoo.
With regard to the former, that is the Bomarc, the details were given by the government, and that document is to be found in the Canada treaty series. I regret I do not have the date. The one dealing with the Voodoo, which is part of the triangular swap deal, was published as No. 5 of the Canada treaty series, of June 12, 1961. None of these involved the disclosure of information which could be prejudicial to national security.
In the course of his remarks the hon. gentleman said that Canada was becoming a junior partner in arrangements to establish nuclear weapons on our soil without our having complete control over them. The hon. gentleman, for whom I have a high regard, will not misunderstand me when I say I thought this was a very strange argument to come from him, because of his sincere desire, which I share, that there should be a limit on the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The logic of my hon. friend's argument is that Canada should have insisted on complete national control over the warheads for the Voodoo and the Bomarc, but the disastrous effect of any such insistance on our part would be to breach a principle underlying all U.S.A. and NATO arrangements concerning nuclear weapons, and which has been unanimously endorsed by the United Nations in the Irish resolution opposing the dissemination of nuclear weapons. Therefore I say that I find this argument coming from him to be a very strange one indeed.

We are not, by the agreement the government signed on August 18, acquiring nuclear weapons. We are not joining the nuclear club. The custody of these nuclear weapons continues to be with the United States. In no sense of the word can we be accused on the basis of this agreement, which has to do with the storage of nuclear weapons for defensive purposes on this continent, and in the case of the CF-104 in Europe as in any way participating in an expansion of the nuclear club.
When my hon. friend says that we do not even know what the arrangements are, to the extent that these arrangements can be spelled out without violating the principles of security I would refer him to the release to which he drew our attention today. The final paragraph of it contains the kind of information, and the only kind of information which the right hon. Leader of the Opposition said in 1959 could be given-
That is a misinterpretation of my remarks.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
-when he presaged what would happen. That is what the right hon. gentleman said. I have reread what he said and I cannot agree with the observation which he now makes. Here is what the release says:
When the stockpiles are established, the warheads will remain in United States custody, and tor this purpose small units of United States custodial personnel will be stationed at the Canadian storage sites, at bases which will of course remain under Canadian command and control. With custody remaining with the United States, the arrangement does not add to the numbers of governments having nuclear weapons at their independent disposal.
-which is the purport of the Irish resolution.
It is also to be noted that provision is made for the application at all times of the most stringent safety measures. Finally, these nuclear warheads cannot be used operationally without the authorization of the Canadian government. Joint control is thus assured.
My hon. friend says that the argument on which the government bases its case, namely, that commitments were made by the previous administration, is no excuse for going on with the role. I would ask him to be good enough to recall what I placed on Hansard when I reported the conclusions of the NATO ministerial meeting of last May. What I said will be found in Hansard of May 27 last at page 305, and I think what I said then is relevant to the discussion now before us:
I want to make perfectly clear that Canada has undertaken no new commitments at the meeting just concluded. It is, however, the policy of this government to take the steps needed to make it possible for the Canadian forces to discharge the role accepted for them by the previous government. This was as long ago as 1959. That role would not disappear if Canada failed to carry it
Interim. Supply
out; all that would happen would be that some other member or members of the alliance would have to shoulder the obligation in our place.
The kind of forces Canada agreed to contribute were to meet part of an established NATO military requirement, and I am sure that no hon. member of this house would wish Canada to be placed in the position where it would be foisting upon others a task voluntarily assumed by Canada through the former government as part of the collective defence effort of the alliance.
So, I believe the argument of commitment is relevant. The honour of the nation was at stake. The extent of our participation in the alliance is involved. The question of our relations, not only with the United States but with the other members of the NATO alliance, is definitely involved. These were the considerations that the right hon. gentleman opposite I am sure had in mind when he spoke about this matter as he did in 1959 and which we, confronted with the responsibility, had to consider with regard to this very important matter.
The hon. gentleman said today, and I can well understand this observation, that since the international situation seems to have changed, the nuclear role was now meaningless. I will at once admit that if one could see the evolving events following the signing of the test ban agreement, he might find some comfort in the observations of the hon. gentleman. But what are the facts? The facts are that the test ban agreement, important achievement that it is, marking an obvious and sincere detente, I think, between the Soviet union and the United States in particular, the Soviet union and the United Kingdom, the United States and the western world generally, was made possible not only because of a willingness on the part of the Soviet union to sign this agreement with regard to the three environments involved, but it was encouraged strongly, I suggest, by the events of last November arising over what Mr. Gromyko called the other day in the United Nations the Caribbean situation or, more particularly, the situation arising out of the placing of offensive nuclear weapons on the soil of Cuba not far from the shores of North America, and also by the fact that the Soviet union is absorbed with other important considerations.
I say all this without in any way wishing to depreciate the extent of the steps that have been taken in the newly evolving understanding between the Soviet union and the west. But I think it may well be argued that we have been able in part to achieve this happy situation, which we hope will continue to grow, as a result of the fact that we in the west were able to argue from a position of strength. In the face of the present world

Interim Supply
situation one must not forget that this situation governs international relations, regrettable as that may be.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman mentioned something about the efforts being made to reduce the nuclear armaments that now confront both east and west. All of us in this country are anxious to see progress made in the field of disarmament. But the nuclear test ban treaty is not a disarmament treaty. It is an arrangement outside of the consideration that now governs the deliberations of the 18 nations who have been conferring in Geneva and who, I hope, shortly after the conclusion of the disarmament discussions in the present general assembly of the United Nations will return to their task. I do not deny that the test ban treaty may be an encouragement for success in these disarmament deliberations. But does anyone seriously argue that the policy of the government of Canada is inconsistent in any way with the desire of this country and of the people of the west under conditions of security to minimize the occasion of war by accident or by miscalculation merely because we resort to steps which I believe have been partly responsible for our ability to sit down at the bargaining table and bargain from a position of strength?
If one were to adopt that argument, he would have to apply it to every member of the NATO alliance; and it must not be forgotten that in the important talks which have been taking place between the three great powers in Europe, two of them are members of the NATO alliance and share much greater burdens in that alliance than does Canada, great as is our obligation and burden. We will work for disarmament. We will recognize the difficulty of achieving it in the face of an absence of decision with regard to the major political problems that divide east and west. But we will pursue every course that we can, through our spokesman in the person of General Burns, to try and bring about some understanding that will add to the detente which now seemingly is under way between the Soviet union and the nations of the west.
I would suggest that there is reason for optimism. There is reason for believing that some progress can be made. There is reason for believing that it can be made before the meeting in Geneva of the 18 states of the disarmament committee shortly after the general assembly of the United Nations. There are three areas now in this field of disarmament in which I think we should strive for agreement at the earliest possible moment. These have been mentioned by the President of the United States, they have been referred to by the foreign minister of the Soviet union,

and the day before yesterday they were underlined by Lord Home, the foreign minister for the United Kingdom. They are, first, an agreement by the United States and by the Soviet union for the outlawing of nuclear weapons in outer space. Second, the establishment of control posts and inspection teams on both sides of the iron curtain; and third, steps to be taken for the non-dissemination of nuclear weapons. Those are the three areas of possible agreement, one of them, I hope within the course of the next two or three months, the other two possibly only at Geneva. They are far from being a comprehensive disarmament arrangement but they do represent important steps. The one having to do with the placing of inspection teams would serve to eliminate the possibility of surprise attack. In the growing understanding, which I believe to be solid and which I hope will continue to be firm and represent a sincere desire on both sides, we must recognize the limitations which confront those countries who have not yet had placed before them the ultimate result of this detente. So I say to the hon. gentleman-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question? I am just wondering, with regard to the third area in the disarmament conference proceedings, the prevention of the further dissemination of nuclear weapons, would he say that Canada is now going to be able to argue from strength, having agreed to have nuclear weapons placed on her soil?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Certainly. Nothing that we are doing in the policy that has been announced by the government, as I said a moment ago, is contrary to the Irish resolution which deals with the non-dissemination of nuclear weapons. There is nothing inconsistent between the policy of this government and that resolution. We have not joined the nuclear club. The custody of these weapons will be, and will continue to be with, the United States. It is only when there is a question of operational use that the element of joint control arises.
These are the facts. I know my hon. friend, is sincere in this matter. Over many years I have had with him a community of interest in this problem. He and I and a former member for Greenwood, Mr. Denton Massey, went as young members from this house to Geneva to join with the voices of other young people from this country and the world to try to bring about some understanding between peoples of various countries on both sides of the iron curtain. Nothing that we are doing in this policy, nothing that this government, headed by the right hon. gentleman who has done so much for peace and for the United.

Nations, is doing can in any way be regarded as an abrogation of these ideals and these former efforts.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. gentleman would permit one more question for clarification. What does he mean by the dissemination of nuclear weapons? Does he mean the dispersal of them in other countries than the United States, Great Britain and Russia, or is there some other meaning attached to this term?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, there is no hidden meaning. The nondissemination of nuclear weapons is defined in the resolution introduced by the ambassador for Ireland at the United Nations two years ago. Canada subscribed to that resolution. An analysis of the resolution will show that present government policy is perfectly consistent with it. That resolution sought to limit the number of nations with nuclear weapons under independent control. Only four countries in the world now have that kind of nuclear capacity. Canada is not one of them. As I have argued tonight, I hope sincerely and with moderation, that is the position of the government. I believe that is the position of this house. That is the position which is embodied in the government's policy.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to detain the committee for only a few minutes. I just want to say that in my opinion the minister has made a very sincere attempt to defend a position which is indefensible. He tells this committee that, having himself on behalf of the government signed an agreement for the acquisition of nuclear arms for Canadian forces, this does not make Canada a nuclear power; nor does it entail Canada joining the nuclear club.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit me to make one intervention here? I did not say that we had an agreement for acquiring nuclear weapons. I said we had an agreement with the United States with regard to the storage of nuclear weapons for Canadian forces.

The Secretary of State for External Affairs has signed on behalf of the government an agreement under which Canada acquires nuclear warheads on Canadian soil under the custody of United States military forces. He says that this does not mean we have become a nuclear power and it does not mean we have joined the nuclear club. I wonder whether the Secretary of State for External Affairs really thinks that
Interim Supply
anyone will accept this kind of hocus pocus. The government of Canada may say that this does not make us a nuclear power and that it does not mean we have joined the nuclear club, but certainly the attitude of other nations will be that we have become a nuclear power and that we have joined the nuclear club. The mere fact that these nuclear weapons are under the partial custody of the United States does not remove the fact that they are on Canadian soil and are in the hands of Canadian forces.
May I remind the committee that it is not many months ago that nuclear weapons were placed in Cuba; they were not in the hands of Cuban forces, they were in the hands of Soviet forces. This did not stop the United States and ourselves and other members of the western alliance from being alarmed that nuclear arms were in Cuba. We did not take the position that because nuclear arms were in the custody of Soviet forces Cuba had not joined the nuclear club and constituted no threat to western hemispheric security. Not at all; we took the position that they should get those nuclear arms out of Cuba, and get them out fast. The minister is not fooling anyone by saying that, because these warheads are in United States custody, this does not put us in the class of being members of the nuclear club or make us members of a nuclear society. As a matter of fact it is only a year and a half ago that the Liberal party was taking the position that the acquisition of nuclear arms by the Conservative administration would have made Canada a nuclear power and would have put her into the nuclear club.
The other thing is that the Secretary of State for External Affairs made mention of the fact that I had criticized or referred to our being a junior member of a nuclear complex with the United States. I certainly was not suggesting that nuclear arms should be in Canada solely under Canadian control. My statement at that time related to a quotation from the book "The Liberal Party" written by the Hon. J. W. Pickersgill, in which he said that the Liberal party was opposed to accepting nuclear weapons, not only because it was not a suitable role for Canada and would lessen the chances of peace, but because there was no possibility of Canada having custody, and therefore we would be surrendering part of our national sovereignty. My objection was to Canada's surrendering part of its national sovereignty without reference to parliament.
The secretary of state has gone all around the subject and not dealt with the main question I raised. I was not saying that we had never discussed nuclear arms in this house.

I agree that the government went to the country last April and that the present Prime Minister, as leader of the Liberal party, announced that if his government were elected they were prepared to enter into some type of agreement for nuclear arms. It seems to me amazing that a party which has talked so much about the supremacy of parliament should now be beating all around the bush talking about disarmament and the hopes for the future, talking about everything except the subject relevant to this discussion, namely, why has the government not given this parliament an opportunity to approve and ratify this agreement?
