I am sorry to interrupt such an interesting discussion as the one which is before the committee at the present time but I should like to take this opportunity to protest another of the ill-conceived and discriminatory pieces of legislation which have gone to make up the Pearson plan. I refer to the legislation setting up designated or distressed areas in Canada as announced in a press release on September 6 by the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Industry. At that time some 35 designated or distressed areas in Canada would qualify, it was stated, for special measures of federal assistance.
I point out, first of all, that this was announced in a press release. That is how we seem to find out about most things. I had to get my copy by coming to Ottawa; I do not think any hon. member of this house received a copy of the release. I know that

some hon. members were very much interested in this question as it affects southwestern Ontario. I am thinking, in particular, of the hon. member for Waterloo South who, I am sorry to learn, is ill and unable to be with us. I know that the hon. member for Perth, the hon. member for Oxford, the hon. member for Wellington-Huron, Waterloo North and others did not receive copies of this press release.
Even the mayors of the municipalities concerned were not notified. What did they have to say? I should like to read from the Guelph daily Mercury of September 12, in which the mayor of Guelph had this comment to make:
The federal government should at least tell the public what constitutes a depressed area, what special considerations are involved and when this became effective.
The report continued:
When the depressed areas were first announced, the mayor of Brantford was surprised to know he was living in one. It should be publicly known just what constitutes a depressed area.
Having in mind the public relations branches attached to the two departments of government concerned, I think the least that could have been done was to have advised every member of this house of this important piece of proposed legislation.
What are likely to be the effects of this measure? I am speaking not only as one who represents a particular area of Canada. This proposal affects all areas of Canada. This ill-conceived piece of legislation, like so many others introduced by this fumbling and bumbling government, was certainly not carefully studied or considered before it was introduced. The government did not take time to analyse the conditions which cause depression and, above all, did not stop to consider what reaction the designation of a particular area in the heart of an industrial district might have on neighbouring cities within a few miles of each other. For example, let us suppose we have a father with four children. They are all in one room and the father gives one of the children a ten dollar bill without giving the others anything. You have a family row on your hands immediately.
Here we find a similar situation. Guelph, Hamilton, Kitchener, Waterloo, Stratford, Preston and many other smaller communities were all one happy family in this area. The government has given to the city of Brantford concessions, in this case worth $400,000 to one particular industry. Similar concessions are not available to the other members of this happy family of towns which are all in that area-towns which had been getting along nicely and which have been competitive in
Interim Supply
getting industry and in improving economic conditions. They were getting along well until this government interfered.
Let us review the steps leading up to the introduction of this discriminatory legislation. It was announced on September 6. The criteria for designation were set forth in the same announcement and I think that for the record I should read the main ones. They are these:
A national employment service area qualified as a designated area provided-
(A) it has been classified by the Department of Labour as a labour surplus area for one half or more of the summer months (May to October) during the past eight years; and it has experienced an employment increase of less than one half the national average over the same period; or-
So it goes on, with "and" and "or" and "or" and "and". If you can understand it, you are better than I am at deciphering things, Mr. Chairman. However, no consideration is given to the present or future employment potential of an area.
I should like to read, now, from a brief presented to the Minister of Industry in connection with this discriminatory move. This is a brief which was presented to the Minister of Industry by the mayors and reeves of the municipalities concerned. It states:
As you, Mr. Minister, know, farm machinery manufacturing has long been a major industry in Brantford and to some extent must bear the blame for some of the gyrations that the city of Brantford has experienced. But surely some of the misfortunes that have befallen Brantford during the past five years were unique and by this we mean the closing of the Cockshutt plow plant several years ago. and the razing of the Massey Ferguson's Market street plant. But the fact that these industries are now being replaced by new plants must certainly be considered now. It is known that a new $13,000,000 Massey Ferguson plant is under construction at the present, as well as a new division of Cockshutt Farm Equipment, which is now a subsidiary of Oliver Farm Corp., U.S.A. The increases in employment and assessment that will result from the construction of these two plants and their eventual operation will, no doubt, once again put the Brantford area in the vanguard of progressive communities in southern Ontario.
So nothing was said in the criteria about the present or future potential with respect to the employment picture. Then we move along to the time after the announcement was made and the criteria were laid out. The policy of the government was that of central control and sidestepping the municipalities and the province. The government took the matter into its own hands and said to Brantford: We will name you a designated area. The municipality was not consulted.
The government also sidestepped provincial autonomy. Just a few years ago the provincial government brought in legislation to prevent municipalities competing with one another for industries. The situation had got to the

Interim Supply
point where a municipality would offer an industry freedom from municipal taxes for so many years in order to entice it to come to that area. This went on and on until things got out of hand. The provincial government then said: No, this must stop; and legislation was passed to that end. Here we have the federal government stepping in, going over the provincial legislation and saying: Brantford, you are a designated area and we will give you this and that.
The federal government is sidestepping municipal autonomy. They are not even consulting the municipalities. They are not even asking them: Do you want to become a designated area or not? In the criteria that have been established, too much emphasis has been placed upon statistics. I should like to place on the record an editorial headed "... and Statistics", which appeared in the Guelph Guardian of October 2, 1963. It reads:
Brantford may well be statistically a depressed area according to the formula used by Ottawa to determine that state of affairs; but if it is, then the formula should be changed.
It is absurd for the taxpayer to foot the bill to give industries concessions amounting to more than $400,000 to establish in Brantford, rather than in Guelph or some other community.
There are said to be lies, damned lies and statistics. It is only on the basis of far from convincing statistics that tax money is being used in this curious way.
Under the principle of cabinet solidarity the government presumably is in accord with the answer given the delegation from this area by the minister they interviewed, the Hon. Charles M. Drury, who represents Montreal St. Antoine-West-mount. Mr. Drury simply stands or falls by the statistics. It is a reasonable prediction that such simple faith in statistics will lead the minister into more troubles than his ability will get him out of.
This is a case of a statesmanlike measure being applied in anything but statesmanlike fashion. There would be little objection to the taxpayer's money being used to transfer plants to, say, a one industry town that had lost that industry; or to a community under special difficulties which could not provide a reasonable standard of living for its citizens.
But Brantford is a highly industrialized city vith higher wage rates, for instance, than Guelph, and certainly no greater unemployment problem than this or many other cities. Reconsideration of the policy is urgently necessary, and the sooner the better.
And so these were the steps taken. How does this affect a community? I can give you a concrete example of just how it has affected the city I represent, Guelph. Last August it was announced by the city that a company was coming into our community. A lease was signed for 10 years. A few weeks ago the contractor had the footings in and the ground plumbing installed. Two thirds of the steel was on site. Overnight the company heard that if they went to Brantford, a designated area, they could receive concessions up to

$400,000 over the next five years. These concessions are arrived at by taking into account the legislation which provides a three year holiday from income tax, a 50 per cent writeoff on new machinery and a 20 per cent writeoff on buildings. You cannot blame the company for taking advantage of these concessions which have been handed to it on a silver platter.
Here we are, as citizens and taxpayers of that great metropolitan area of western Ontario, contributing taxes to the federal government so that we can sit back and whistle and watch factories going over to the Brantford area, and this after we in our area and many other areas throughout the region have developed an industrial basin and have spent millions of dollars to attract new industries. We were aggressive. We worked hard to build up these industrial basins and now we must sit back and watch industries flit by our doors on the way over to establish themselves in Brantford.
I ask the minister to reconsider this discriminatory piece of legislation; and when amendments to the Income Tax Act come before this house, to make possible these provisions for depressed areas, I hope hon. members will think twice before they vote for such amendments to the act.
I point out to members from industrial areas that something else can happen. Do you know that an old, established industry in your city can move to a designated area, change its name, build a new factory, put in new machinery and make a new product and thus be eligible for these concessions? I say to any member who has an industry in his riding that that industry can move to a designated area and get these concessions.
Some may say that if I were a member for a designated area the situation might work in reverse. Yes, it can work that way. A member can represent a designated area tonight and tomorrow morning on the say-so of the government it will no longer be a designated area. You may have been negotiating with a company previously to come to your riding and establish a plant. You may spend one to two years trying to get the company to to your area as a designated area; but then overnight by the stroke of a pen you are no longer a designated area and all your work is of no use. It works both ways.
Briefly that is the situation. In conclusion, I would ask the government, particularly the Minister of Industry, to revise their thinking as to this type of legislation. First of all, respect municipal autonomy. Consult the municipalities and ask them if they want to be designated areas. Revise the criteria by

which a designated area is established. I think we will all agree in principle that there are areas in Canada in need of help, but let those areas come to Ottawa and ask for assistance. Do not put so much emphasis on statistics but rather on the practical application of the scheme. Think about the distance between a designated area and non-des-ignated areas. Keep out of highly industrialized areas. I do not think for a minute that this legislation was ever intended to apply to a highly industrialized area and thus start a family row among all the cities and communities in that area. Do not override the provincial legislation already in effect. These areas should not be selected on a patronage basis. I am not accusing the government of doing that, but I do say that 63 per cent of these designated areas in Ontario have Liberal members. There are five areas that have Liberal members, two are Conservative ridings, while one is an N.P.D. riding. I say that 63 per cent of the designated areas in Ontario are represented by Liberal members or Liberal senators.
The government should prevent further steals of industry from one city to another. If you want to help this situation, then help move the employees from one area to the other. The area of which I am speaking covers a radius of 25 miles, and today people can commute easily. If there is a need for help in one area, it is not a problem for people to commute a short distance like that.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I would say to this government they should do one of two things. They should either remove Brantford from the list of designated areas, or give the rest of us in southwestern Ontario the same concessions. We would rather not have these concessions. It hurts our pride. We do not not want this help. We would rather go it alone. We are not happy about the cartoon published in the Globe and Mail which showed the mayors of all these municipalities playing violins in the street and begging for support. We would rather go it alone and get industry into these areas as we have done in the past. This problem requires immediate and serious thought on the part of the government, which introduced this legislation in a hasty and ill-considered manner in order to beat the 60 days of decision. Then they found themselves in a real muddle. If you do not believe me, just go into southwestern Ontario, and talk to the people in the area to which I have been referring and have the honour to represent.

If this office had been established, I am afraid that every citizen in Red Deer would be appealing to him tomorrow because of the injustices that have been perpetrated upon them in the last couple of days. The reason for this is simply the bureaucratic actions of

government departments, in this case the bungling and inefficient administration of the transport and defence departments in relation to the Penhold air base and its development into a jet training base.
As long ago as seven years, plans were being made to develop this important training centre into a jet training base. At that time the government was well aware of the implications that would be brought about through the newer developments in aircraft training. This awareness carried right on through the Conservative government's administration. These plans have finally come to a head. This meant the purchasing of the Tudor jet aircraft which would lead to a program whereby young men would go directly into training on jet aircraft. In recent months plans developed to the point where the government, carrying through the policies of the previous government, had let the tenders for the construction of the necessary runways. The tenders had been opened, and even the treasury board had considered the expenditure of approximately $3 million, or, to be exact $2.8 million for this purpose. The contractor concerned had moved in equipment planning to begin work on runway construction. In addition to this, the air force moved in a lot of equipment. Not only that, but they had called for a program of additional housing in the city of Red Deer which, just the night before last, was cancelled. Last Monday night the city council had given approval for this $1 million housing program. As late as three weeks ago, both the mayor of Red Deer and myself were informed that this program was going to go through, and we were informed by the defence department.
Then, suddenly the project was withdrawn. What has been the result? Well, the contractor has lost thousands of dollars because the contract that had been more or less assured has been cancelled. We find that a $1 million housing project has likewise been cancelled after the city had reserved the area and made the necessary plans to supply the essential services. The whole community of central Alberta is upset because of this decision reversal.
We investigated and we have found out that as long as nine months ago negotiations had been carried on by the two departments concerned, at departmental level, regarding the safety requirements relating to air traffic lanes and buffer zones. All through these discussions it had seemed to the air force that they would be going forward with the project, and the outline I have given is proof of that. Then all of a sudden a new regulation was introduced and this regulation or recommendation-no matter what it is called it amounts to the same thing-set up a 20 mile

buffer zone on either side of the normal air traffic lane, making it absolutely impractical for the air force to use this area as a training centre, because the air space was not sufficient for the high speed aircraft involved.
What is the result? It is a waste of taxpayers' money. It has caused a great deal of confusion and distress for a great many of our citizens. Half the village of Penhold will find itself empty because the people living there are working at the air base. Many of them will have to move elsewhere or become unemployed in the city of Red Deer. In the case of Penhold debentures were floated in order to provide the essential services for a housing program. These will have to be cancelled, and now the village is in extreme financial difficulties, and is even facing the threat of bankruptcy. This is the problem we find because there is not the proper consultation and co-ordination between two government departments that there should be. This is the danger that is involved when governments become as vast as they have become today.
I demand that the government publicly and fully make known what has happened in this matter, and that appropriate action be taken to clear up what appears to be vast interdepartmental blundering.
This is only an illustration concerning one constituency of the chaos that exists between all levels of government. One department simply does not know what another is doing. Were I to go into the number of instances where provincial and federal government programs do not coincide and are not coordinated, I could take more time than the rules of the house allow. We have already seen first rate examples during this session of parliament.
The Canada pension plan, introduced with such a flourish a few months ago, is now in a position where the government cannot go forward with it without the co-operation of a single provincial government. We, the duly elected members of the house find that we have been wasting our breath, time and efforts becoming acquainted with this vast subject, because in the end we have found that the future of this proposal does not depend on our efforts but on the whim of a single provincial government.

Another example is the municipal loan fund. This was also introduced with a great flourish. When he spoke about it in the city of Toronto the Prime Minister said something like this, "Come on and get it boys. It is here for you." However it did not take very long before it was discovered there were problems relating to it, and a conference of provincial premiers had to be called. As a result this loan fund has not been implemented in the way it should have been, nor has it met with needs it was intended to meet.
What could be a better example of this bungling between governments, provincial and federal, than that set forth by the hon. member who preceded me when he spoke about assistance for distressed areas? How does the federal government know which area in any province is a distressed area? I can give an example in my own province. One particular town has been named. I do not deny that that town is not in a needy area, but what about the other areas adjacent to it? What about other areas in other parts of the province?
Penhold.

Yes, Penhold will be one too, unless something is done. How can the federal government know the needs of the municipalities, and what right has it to designate, over and above the authority of a province, what is a special, needy area? This is just another illustration of the problems we face when there is not adequate consultation between governments at the various levels.
I can give another illustration. What about the history of the Columbia river treaty? How long has it been held up for this very same reason? Because there has not been proper co-ordination, discussion and planning between the provincial government and the federal government, the result is that the economy of the nation is held back.
The announcement of bold plans that quite obviously affect provincial governments, before those governments have been consulted, has led to a great sense of ill-will on the part of provincial governments towards the federal government, and what better illustration of that could we find at present than the province of Quebec? The need for government by consultation is one of the most urgent things facing us.

I have previously demanded that the government establish a department of federal-provincial affairs. It should be a full-scale ministry, having the prime purpose of dealing with those matters that concern the different levels of government, federal and provincial, and the provinces one with another on a broader scale. To me it seems just as important that the provinces be consulted, ahead of time, on matters of federal action and policy that will affect them, as it is that every piece of legislation and order in council be examined to assure conformity with the Canadian Bill of Rights. The need is self-evident and does not require further emphasis from me at this time.
Several provinces have seen the need for such a department and have themselves set up departments of provincial-federal affairs. If that could be done in every province, with the lead being given by the federal government, then how much easier would it be to deal with the problems that resolve around legislation such as the Canada pension plan, the municipal development fund, and that relating to distressed areas? We must have an even greater degree of co-operation in the future between the provinces and the federal government. We all realize that it will not be too long before a power grid is necessary across the whole country. We know we are in desperate need today of a national highways program. What about the tax sharing problem? I am sure the Minister of Finance realizes this better than any of us in the house at this time.
If we are going to have unity-and I mean unity of purpose-among the different levels of government in this land, if we are going to avoid the faux pas and cost to the taxpayers caused by the bumbling and the rivalries between different levels of government that go on at the present time; if we are going to avoid a potent source of friction between provinces and the federal government; if we are to make the whole machinery of government run smoothly at all levels in Canada, then I say a department of federal-provincial affairs within this government is a necessity.

referring to the remarks made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare just the other day, when she said that it depends upon the provincial government of Ontario whether they are going to be able to go forward with the Canada pension plan at all.
I am in slight disagreement with the hon. member. I think there is more than one, and I am glad he has enlightened me as to which one he thought it was. I thought it was Quebec.
I was referring to a specific instance, Mr. Chairman, and I am correct in that reference. If there are other provinces so involved, then the hon. member can make his own speech about them.

Mr. Chairman, in speaking on this interim supply motion I feel it my duty as member of parliament for Waterloo North to express my views and those of others in the house on behalf of my industrial area and the surrounding districts, especially with regard to the designation of depressed areas which was so well explained by the hon. member for Wellington South.
The Minister of Industry has been advised of the storm of regional protest by a protest delegation which came to Ottawa last Friday. This delegation was arranged by my friend and neighbour the hon. member for Wellington South, whose city of Guelph was first affected in our area by the designation of certain industrial centres as "depressed" or "slow growth" areas. The method being followed by this government in applying these regulations is typical of the method they have followed in other fields, such as the pension plan. There is a lack of consideration and consultation. Under the previous government, experts were sent into these areas to be designated as labour surplus areas. These

experts consulted with municipal authorities; they consulted with the officials of the national employment service; they talked to industrialists and businessmen.
The present government has not seen fit to follow this procedure. As usual, they are in too much of a hurry to do the job properly. As a result we have had the same confusion, misunderstanding and complaints surrounding the application of this measure as we have had with such measures as the municipal loans program and the winter works program. It is surprising that this government does not seem able to undertake the most ordinary and routine administrative responsibilities without botching up the job. When they bring in legislation, they cannot get it accepted. An example of this, of course, is the budget, with regard to which they had to withdraw, retreat or revise their original plans.
With regard to depressed areas, these are important measures brought forward by the Waterloo and Kitchener city councils as well as many others in my area. Such proposed legislation could, and will, affect the economy of our country. It is impossible to get business by panic methods. Evidently the watchword of this government is "scramble". They scrambled up the municipal loans program; they scrambled up the pension scheme; they gave us a scrambled budget, and now they are scrambling up this distressed area measure. Everywhere it has been applied, it has caused distress.
Consider the situation in Brantford, Guelph, Kitchener, Galt, Waterloo, Hespeler, and my home town of Elmira. I am sure that if the hon. member for Waterloo South were here he would explain the situation in this way, as would the hon. member for Wellington South.
If there had been even a minimum of consultation with local authorities this situation would not have arisen. There was none of this trouble with the previous Minister of Labour. There were no complaints from the provinces; there were no complaints from the municipalities. The present government set up a new department to handle things formerly handled by the Minister of Labour, together with his other duties. The result has been only to add to the confusion. During the debate on the measure to appoint a Minister of Industry I suggested that this minister look after this department and not try also to cover the work of defence production. After seeing what has happened during the last two or three weeks I believe my suggestion at that time was a good one and the fears I expressed have become reality. There should be one job for one man.
My complaints do not originate with the opposition. There is no obstruction here. These

are complaints originating with responsible municipal and civic bodies, people who have no partisan axe to grind, people who have an interest in the prosperity and welfare of their particular municipalities. These are people who feel that a decision such as that designating a distressed area in my district and other places, without consultation, is doing damage to the Canadian economy at the provincial, municipal and national levels.
Other legislation that has brought criticism is shortening the season for the winter works program by six weeks. Mr. Chairman, they have courses with essentially the same school program as the former government, but with no new schools being built this winter. The tax on building materials was vigorously protested by the Kitchener-Waterloo home builders association and other people across Canada. All these things, rather than helping the economy are making it that much more difficult for provinces and municipalities to cope with their problems.
Resolutions from the twin cities mayors and councils, and others in my area, have been sent to the Prime Minister, the Minister of Industry and other members in the House of Commons. These resolutions have strongly opposed the announced intention of the government of Canada to include the city of Brantford as a designated depressed area.
While agreeing in principle with the necessity of some type of assistance for fully qualified depressed areas, these councils oppose the designation of Brantford as a depressed area, which designation is apparently based on unemployment statistics in the past, with no other factor being considered, including present and future employment potential.
Further, these councils feel that the other designated depressed areas in southern Ontario should be revised to include only those making convincing representations to the federal government and proving actual distressed conditions. The Kitchener-Waterloo Record of Tuesday, October 2, 1963, in an editorial had this to say:
Seven municipalities in the Grand River valley complex are combining to battle the federal government on its recent designation of Brantford as a distressed area. They are afraid they will lose industries to Brantford under the special assistance offered to plants to locate in the officially named area. The opposition is understandable.
Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt in my mind that such legislation would rule out future fair competition for industry, and in such industrialized areas as Waterloo North and Wellington South, where progress and stability are combined, this would be disastrous. May I ask the Minister of Industry to give this matter a second look-yes, a very serious second look.
Interim Supply
Mayor Bauer of Waterloo has summed up this criticism with a sound explanation. He said he could not understand why Brantford is classed as a distressed area because two industries from there are advertising in the Kitchener-Waterloo Record for labour help. Mr. Chairman, surely such remarks should make the minister sit up and take notice regarding this serious problem.

Mr. Chairman, may I use this opportunity to bring to the attention of the committee, in particular to the attention of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, a matter which affects several thousand people in this country. I refer to the fact that a great many immigrants to Canada are denied citizenship because of the arbitrary power given to the minister by section 10 of the Canadian Citizenship Act. Not only can the minister, one man, by himself deny applications for citizenship but, what is worse, he does not have to give any reason for his denial. It seems to me that this is arbitrary authority of the worst kind and runs counter to what we generally consider to be the best principles of British justice.
There are undoubtedly reasons for denying citizenship to some persons. They may not have learned either of our two official languages or they may have criminal records, which it seems to me constitute valid reasons for denying citizenship. But we know that persons are denied citizenship because of their membership in certain social and political organizations, and it is about this that I wish to speak at the moment. This was admitted a year ago when the then minister of citizenship and immigration replied to a question put at that time by the hon. member for Kootenay West. Here I quote from a news story which refers to the reply given by the minister to the hon. member. It is dated April 5, 1962, and is a United Press dispatch:
The federal government has disclosed that membership or association with organizations believed to be subversive could bar new Canadians from obtaining citizenship.
Immigration minister Ellen Fairclough, in a written reply to a question asked in the Commons, said such membership or association was taken into consideration when deciding whether applicants had "an adequate knowledge of the privileges and responsibilities of Canadain citizenship."
Mrs. Fairclough revealed that from January 1947, when the citizenship act came into force, until January 1 last 3,317 applications for citizenship had been rejected and 582,299 granted.
As far as I know, there has never been published a list of those organizations considered to be subversive. In this respect the government of the United States is more forthright than we are. They do publish such a list. I do not know which persons determine which organizations are considered to be subversive and undesirable, but at least a new

Interim Supply
immigrant to the United States knows where he stands. If the Canadian government authorities in charge of these matters feel that certain organizations, political as well as social, are subversive, then I think we ought to know about them. Perhaps we should go further: if they are undesirable and subversive they should be made illegal. I would remind you, Mr. Chairman, that as we stand at the moment even the communist party of Canada is not an illegal organization. But the fact is that citizenship is denied people because they belong to certain organizations, and we are never told what these organizations are.
I complain, Mr. Chairman, that the minister is vested with arbitrary power. To make matters worse, there is no appeal from his authority. Over 3,000 persons have been refused citizenship since 1947, and we assume that a great many of them have been denied citizenship because of membership in certain organizations. Many of these persons have resided in Canada for many years, some for 40 or 45 years. There are many specific cases here which could be cited. If a person is not ready for citizenship after all that time in Canada, then perhaps the logical thing to do is to send him out of Canada.
I believe there has been general satisfaction with the new Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. A number of members have told me that he has given very sympathic hearing to individual cases involving immigration and citizenship matters-cases which members have taken to him. In fact, I understand that he has personally reviewed many cases where he felt an injustice had been done. But I think that we need more than a sympathetic minister; I think we need a change in the procedure. I think we should have a removal of the arbitrary power of the minister. I also feel, along with that, that there should be a right of appeal from a denial of citizenship, and preferably a right of appeal to a judicial body, to a court, rather than to an administrative agency. And it would follow that when Canadian citizenship is denied, a person should know why he is being refused.
The present minister was in Vancouver recently, and on September 23 spoke to the Chinese community there. As hon. members know, the Canadian Chinese have suffered certain discrimination regarding immigration. The minister seems to be taking a sincere interest in removing these discriminations, and I should like to conclude with a short quotation from his speech to the Chinese community of Vancouver at that time. He said:
I have been distressed by the accusations of discrimination which have reached me. If prejudice exists in immigration matters it must be eliminated. True Canadianism permits no discrimination.
[Mr. Prittie.l
All citizens are equal in rights and responsibilities, regardless of ethnic origin or creed. It is with this view in mind that I am most sincere in my effort to weed out discrimination and prejudice.
You can count on me to work in the interests of all ethnic groups and to seek a fair and just solution to the vexing problem of Chinese immigration to Canada.
I like the attitude of the minister in these matters, and my only purpose in speaking this evening is to urge on the minister and his cabinet colleagues a review of this situation whereby arbitrary power is held by the department to refuse citizenship, and to set up fair procedures and let people know where they stand. I think that we have to do away with the type of system we have at the present time, where an informer can inform the department of the activities of certain persons but never has to face the person upon whom he has informed. I would appreciate very much if the government would take under consideration a reform of the procedures for applications for citizenship.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to inform the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond that I will certainly bring his comments to the minister's attention. I am sure the minister would want me to indicate his gratitude for the kind references he has made.

Mr. Chairman, now that we come to the discussion of an expenditure of public funds, and particularly the distribution of these outlays, may I call the attention of the government to the Charlevoix riding which I have been representing for about a year now.
If I call the attention of this house to that county, it is because, in my opinion, it has been forgotten in the last few years in turn by the members of the Conservative and the Liberal administration.
In the course of a speech made during the early part of this session, an hon. member gave us a poetical description of the charms and beautiful scenery of that county, for which I congratulate him.
But, Mr. Chairman, what is spoken of a great deal less, because it is truly shameful for the older parties which are responsible for it, is the economic situation with which the people of that county are trying to cope desperately but without much success.
I can tell the house that, as the member for that riding, I have inherited a dreadful situation, owing to the inefficiency of the previous governments and particularly the representatives of that county.
The county of Charlevoix is one of those in the province of Quebec which suffers most

from that terrible plague called unemployment. That is why I request that this county be included in the designated areas in order to receive special economic benefits.
In that part of the riding which, geographically, makes up the county of Charlevoix live about 8,000 families. The statistics published during the month of March by the La Malbaie unemployment insurance office, indicated that there were then 3,000 unemployed.
That also means hardship, worry and lower standards for those families who have not deserved that fate and I wonder how much longer those people will accept placidly to remain in such conditions.
The economic situation in my county began to go downhill in 1954 and has not improved since, although we have had in office during that period a Liberal, then a Conservative and again a Liberal government.
But what is most urgent today is not so much to determine who is responsible for that situation but rather to face the facts and try to find a solution to the problem.
Many things would have to be done to revive industry in my county. To mention but a few, may I be allowed to say that one reason why trade is slowing down more than anywhere else in that county and why very few industries are going there is that we have no modern or speedy means of transportation to encourage them to do so, apart from the fact that that county is located far from the large centres of the province, in spite of the fact that it has the shortest road to reach the territory where lies the greatest potential in ore and other resources of the province and probably of all Canada as well.
To cope with the situation, and although I do not pretend to be an expert in such things, may I be allowed to suggest that the government should consider the possibility of making highway 15, which goes from Quebec to Seven Islands, and even beyond, a section of the trans-Canada highway. I am sure that it will be proven in the future that such a section would be more useful to Canadians than the present laying-out of the highway on the south shore of the St. Lawrence. Nobody can deny that the territory located on the north shore of the St. Lawrence river, from Quebec city to Labrador, includes many times the land located to the south over the same distance.
Moreover, that territory's natural potential constitutes the determining factor of future economic activity as, up to now, enough of it has been discovered to prove its extraordinary importance.
Interim Supply
It is only logical to reverse, in a suitable way, the present trend which causes the industrial, commercial and tourist traffic to make use of the south shore in order to reach the north shore.
Another suggestion, which could be put into practice immediately would be the removal of the tolls collected for crossing the Saguenay, as they are a hindrance to trade. I have not tried to find out whether these tolls are warranted or not, but I had occasion to ascertain that trailer-trucks had to pay up to $9 to cross the Saguenay, which is about a mile wide.
I suggest consequently that the government should enter into some sort of an agreement with the company concerned and subsidize it, so that these rates could be cut down or altogether abolished. Besides, the government should make a few inquiries about the material and financial possibilities of building a bridge across the Saguenay.
Under the ARDA program, the government would be wise to take stock of the land under cultivation at the present time, so as to decide upon the best methods. In my part of the country, the farmers eke out a bare existence, mostly because there are very few transportation facilities towards the marketing centres.
The harbour facilities in Charlevoix county should be studied and the necessary improvements brought about as soon as possible. Thus, one would kill two birds with one stone, by allowing hundreds of families to find work and, at the same time, by promoting trade in that part of the country. Many harbours and wharves need improvement because they are dilapidated and represent a loss of money for the government. Some money was rightly spent at those places but it would not be reasonable to let them deteriorate and it would be illogical to waste money for their destruction as it is presently done in the case of the wharf at Port-aux-Saumons.
I am thinking for instance of the wharf at Pointe au Pic, the wharf at St. Simeon; those I will only mention to say I appreciate the fact that this government is now spending money appropriated last year for rebuilding. But there are other small wharves such as those at St. Fidele, Ste-Irdnee, Baie Ste Catherine and many other places and there are many wharves which could be useful to facilitate shipping and stimulate the tourist industry. But what is most urgent, in my opinion, is to build a deep water wharf at Baie St. Paul, because this would help the development of the mining industry. An iron mine is now in operation on a very small scale but its production would be increased if the necessary facilities for shipping the

Interim Supply
ore were available. I am informed that it thorough examinations were made other places could be found. On that same subject, concerning the mining industry in my riding, the government should look for means to promote research and prospecting because I have often been told that the rock formations in the Charlevoix hills indicate possible important mineral deposits.
Another way to remedy unemployment in that depressed area would be to promote the tourist industry. There has been a good start, part of which was the building of a landing field at Ste Irenee, which the government should keep in good shape during the winter season. Charlevoix is well known for its unique scenery, its lakes full of fish, its mountains and forests, where one can hunt fine moose and deer-in the proper season, of course. I trust that if the government made the necessary publicity, the tourist industry would develop considerably.
There is another point which I would like to mention. An attempt is being made now, at great cost and with incomplete success, to maintain navigation and keep the Quebec ports open for the whole winter season. With regard to this matter, I would have a suggestion for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcll-raith). He should send some engineers to examine the deep water wharf project undertaken at Beaupre by St. Ann Paper Limited. This wharf, though yet incomplete, might, I think, easily be acquired from the said company and completed, so as to give to the district and city of Quebec a deep water wharf where navigation might be kept open all winter, because the river never completely freezes at that point which is only 20 miles off the city of Quebec. Ships of all sizes might load and unload there all year round. Then, highway 15 becoming the trans-Canada highway, and with the railways serving the district, we would be able to solve that almost insoluble problem of winter navigation in the port of Quebec.
Those, Mr. Chairman, are some suggestions I am making to the government to help it forget the errors of the former administrations which made of the county of Charlevoix one of the least developed areas of the province of Quebec.
I even urge the government to act as quickly as possible in order to rectify the intolerable economic conditions now prevailing in my county of Charlevoix. The suggested projects are by no means all those which the federal government might carry out in my riding-they are mere indications.

Mr. Chairman, during the debate on interim supply, we heard a while ago-and I think this question should be brought up-about the acquisition of nuclear weapons by our country.
Many events took place during the summer. First there was the signing of a nuclear test ban agreement by the big three: the U.S.S.R., the United States and England, and that agreement was approved and signed by several other countries, including Canada. At that time, people were talking of an easing throughout the world and it was said that the cold war was getting hot.
Barely a few days later, our country, in turn, signed with the United States a treaty or a commitment to acquire and stock nuclear weapons on our soil.
Mr. Chairman, I want to point out the nonsense of those two actions. Canada cannot proceed with nuclear tests. Canada is entirely unable to make tests today, and yet she signs the agreement. Whether she signs it or not does not change a thing. Canada never made nuclear tests, she never exploded a nuclear or atomic bomb. She cannot do it. She cannot do it, but the Prime Minister nevertheless signs the agreement. What obligation does that impose on him? He will not explode nuclear weapons. And yet he signs the agreement. He has no risk to run, and he says: "Here, we take part in the easing in the world". He cannot do otherwise, because he is unable to explode a nuclear bomb.
But what he could have done for the easing of the situation, the part he could have played to warm the cold war, was to refuse nuclear weapons. He was able to do that, but he did not do it. He says he will do what he cannot do, but he does not do what he can do. That is exactly what our present government did. It acquired nuclear weapons and it is ready to stock them on Canadian soil.
Well, Mr. Chairman, only a few days after Canada committed itself to acquire nuclear weapons and to store them on our territory, I had the opportunity to attend the annual session of the United Nations. I must say that in the climate prevailing at that time, when every country of the world was talking of eased tension, Canada cut a sorry figure indeed, since our country was the only one in the world to have taken a further step in the direction of nuclear weapons and world destruction, by accepting such weapons on its territory. All the others were talking of disarmament and Canada was the only one, since the signing of the Moscow treaty, to acquire nuclear arms.

What was our position at the United Nations before the other countries of the world? I heard the Prime Minister of Canada make a fine speech, but I could not help thinking: those are only words, words and words, but nothing practical, nothing real, except the acquisition of nuclear weapons by our country and their storage on our territory.
Moreover, Mr. Chairman, two days later, I heard at the annual session of the UN the day after President Kennedy proposed to Russia to co-operate and set up a joint Russian and American expedition to the moon, the minister of external affairs for Dahomey said in very simple terms: "Americans and Russians, when you go up to the moon hand in hand, just ask yourselves then if you have performed your duty towards your brothers remaining on earth." And he added: "For us, the greatest country is not the one who will first land on the moon; for us, Africans, the greatest country in the world is not the one who will have the most destructive bombs, but the greatest country will be the one which will have done the most on earth to fight illness, ignorance, hunger and destitution throughout the world."
Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, there was another member of the house between the Prime Minister and myself and I could not resist looking at him and saying: "That is a role suited for us, a role that we can play. We could fight sickness, ignorance, hunger and misery throughout the world. That is a role cut out for Canada. It is a role for Canadians because we can co-operate in that field instead of trying to find out who will stockpile the greatest number of nuclear bombs in our country, a military role which will inevitably lead us to use those means of destruction one day. On the other hand, if we help other countries and the United Nations to fight sickness, ignorance, hunger and misery, as all other countries advocate, then we will be acting as human beings who are more concerned with the welfare of their fellow men than with knowing whether hay, wheat or barley grows on the moon.
Mr. Chairman, I notice it is ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, before you leave the chair I wonder if I might appeal to the committee to see if there would be any possibility of getting interim supply completed this evening because in order to carry on the business of the country, in order to pay the public servants, it is necessary that this money be voted. We have spent the whole of one day on this subject now, and I wondered if there would be any possibility of getting cooperation to complete interim supply this evening.

Mr. Chairman, I must inform you that we do not intend to end the debate on interim supply either tonight, tomorrow or as long as the privileges and elections committee has not remedied the ridiculous and illogical situation which prevails in this corner of the house. We tried to do it and it was supposed to be done as soon as possible. Last Monday, the house asked that the situation be settled but it has not yet been done. When the committee met this morning, I asked that a solution be found to the problem but nothing was done about it. A resolution was introduced calling for a new meeting of the committee tomorrow morning but it was voted down. The committee is to meet Monday morning. Because of that, the leader of the Ralliement des creditistes and I will have to
Business of the House
make a special trip by automobile at that time to be here for ten o'clock. Well, we are not ready to end the debate tonight.

Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I just wish to ask the house leader to inform us whether he intends to continue with interim supply tomorrow?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. I think the government would have no option but to make every effort to get the necessary funds to carry on the public business of the country which is, of course, the first business of this house.

It being three minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
